This Norway Maple Tree (Acer platanoides) was found in front of Patterson Hall, in Slippery Rock PA. There were multiple types of flora in this area including Tuliptree (Liriodendron tulipifera), Blue Spruce (Picea pungens Engelm), and the invasive Tree-of-Heaven (Ailanthus altissima). The Norway Maple Tree was introduced to Northeastern North America as an invasive species from Europe.

The Norway Maple leaves are opposite and simple. Each leaf is about 4 to 7 inches wide, and posses 5 lobes. The leaves are currently bright green in color. However, once Fall reaches, the leaves will turn bright yellow or orange.

On the ground, I was able to find perfectly in-tact examples of the tree's fruit. The wings of the fruit were extremely wide, almost horizontal.

The bark on this particular tree was light brown in color, and had extremely smooth bark.

During the time of this identification, the temperature was 73 degrees. There was little to no wind, with bright, sunny skies. Humidity was at 82 percent.

description:
The Norway Maple is native to Europe and Western Asia, making it an invasive species, and a part of the Acer genus within the Sapindaceae family. The leaf has a palmate shape with pointed lobes. It was first introduced to North America from England as an ornament plant in the 1700’s, some desired it for its shade cover that it creates with its dense canopy. However, this dense canopy is now an issue to native plants in New England. Norway Maples reproduce in short proximity to each other, causing rapid displacement of native tree and shrubs. Its dense shade covering prevents the growth of other native plants within its vicinity. It is also thought that the Norway Maple produces toxins that prevent the growth of possible native competitors although this has not been proven scientifically.  It is suggested to not plant Norway Maple and to cut down existing trees. Better native substitutes such as the Sugar Maple or the Red Maple are suggested.

Reference: https://www.invasive.org/alien/pubs/midatlantic/acpl.htm

iNaturalist visits Allen Park - Salt Lake City’s newest public space (seven acres) which includes riparian habitat (Emigration Creek); Opened on October 4, 2020 - SLC Public Lands Division. Allen Park was originally founded in the 1930s as a bird sanctuary. Emigration Creek (which also runs through Wasatch Hollow Open Space and Nature Preserve) helps to anchor Allen Park as a riparian habitat - which is very unique and critical for plants and wildlife in an urban setting. 

I went in for a visit on October 13, 2020 and took a preliminary inventory (partial not complete) of what could be observed on an initial walk-through. My observations are summarized as follows. Observers can see Emigration Creek flowing (that is actual water flowing) in several spots along the walkway and it passes underneath the walkway and then runs westward toward the Westminster College area across 1300 East. What is interesting is that Emigration Creek (further upstream) remains “dry” east (and north) within and of Wasatch Hollow Open Space and Nature Preserve. There is a natural spring in Wasatch Hollow Open Space which serves as a water source and feeds into the creek flowing west (and south). There were many kinds of trees: Cottonwoods, Siberia Elms, Locust, Southern Catalpa, and Box Elder Maples, and few Pines and Spruces along the walkway. Many of the Cottonwoods were very large and they ran along the creekside. I could hear several Fox Squirrels and saw one in a tree, but I was not able to take an image. There were also Peafowl on the grounds. I was not able to observe any others birds except for what I am sure were a few Black-capped Chickadees (able to identify by the calls). Temperature was 75 degrees. Winds from south-southwest at 8 mph.

description: Norway maples are deciduous trees that flower in the early spring before the new leaves emerge. They can grow 20-30 meters with grey-brown shallowly grooved bark. The leaves can be large, 7-14 cm tall and 8-20 (but occasionally 25) cm wide. They are opposite, with 5 lobes. Each lobe has one to three teeth. They are very similar in appearance to the sugar maple, but they have white sap and very pointy ends of leaves while the sugar maple has clear sap and can have slightly rounded tips of leaves. They are found all over Europe where they are native, and widely in the U.S. where they were introduced in the 1700s. They are considered invasive in some states because their shallow roots outcompete other plants for moisture. They are found in urban areas along streets and in yards as well as surrounding forests and woodlands. The Norway maple seedminer is a species of moth whose larvae preys on the Norway maple, burrowing into the seeds and eating the buds.

There are probably a couple hundred of them between 2-6" that would be great to remove at this stage. The northern section of the loop is dense with Ligustrum obtusifolium. Besides Carpinus carolinana and a few Viburnum prunifolium, a native understory is non-existent.

description:
Deciduous tree invasive to Rhode Island. Norway maples have large opposite leaves with 7 main points (indicated by the leaf veins on the underside that branch out from one central point). On younger trees, the bark on a Norway maple is grayish and somewhat furrowed with shallow grooves. Norway maples have a thick white sap which is an important distinction between sugar maples (clear watery sap) which the species is commonly mistaken for. The easiest way to identify a Norway maple is to break off a leaf and find the white sap oozing from the stem. 

This Norway maple was observed at URI on the side of Upper College Rd. on the edge of woods next to the sidewalk. Additionally, this tree is infected with Tar spot (black spot on leaf) which is a fungal disease caused by Rhytisma acerinum.
